tip: -세요 (-seyo) respects the subject: 아빠는 가세요 (appaneun gaseyo); for yourself, 가요 (gayo).
높아요 (nopayo) can end a sentence, but in front of a noun the adjective flips to -(으)ㄴ (-(eu)n): 높은 산 (nopeun san) = a high mountain.
헬스장 (helseujang) = gym – Konglish, from English 'health'.
번 (beon) counts times, with native numbers: 두 번 (du beon) = twice.
-아/어서 (-a/eoseo) = so, because: 피곤해서 쉬었어요 (pigonhaeseo swieosseoyo) = tired, so I rested.
-(으)러 가다 (-(eu)reo gada) = go to (do): 보러 갔어요 (boreo gasseoyo) = went to watch.
보다 (boda = than) attaches to what you compare against, and it comes first: 축구보다 야구를 (chukguboda yagureul) = baseball more than soccer – reverse of English order.
치다 (chida) = hit – used for tennis, badminton, piano, guitar: 테니스를 쳐요 (teniseureul chyeoyo).
편 (pyeon) counts films: 세 편 (se pyeon) = three (movies).
좋아해요 (joahaeyo = like) takes 을/를 (eul/reul): 영화를 좋아해요 (yeonghwareul joahaeyo). 좋아요 (joayo = is good) would need 이/가 (i/ga) instead.
없이 (eopsi) = without: 팝콘 없이 (papkon eopsi) = without popcorn.
만에 (mane) = in (just): 하루 만에 (haru mane) = in a single day.
Adjectives built on 있다/없다 take -는 (-neun): 재미있는 책 (jaemiinneun chaek) = an interesting book; most other adjectives take -(으)ㄴ, like 예쁜 (yeppeun).
권 (gwon) counts books: 두 권 (du gwon) = two books.
-기 전에 (-gi jeone) on a verb = before doing it: 자기 전에 (jagi jeone) = before sleeping.
시간 (sigan) counts hours with native numbers: 세 시간 (se sigan) = three hours.
'Good at games' takes the object marker 을/를 in Korean: 게임을 잘해요 (geimeul jalhaeyo) – 잘하다 (jalhada) treats the skill as something you do to the game, no 'at'.
제가 (jega) = 저 (jeo = I) plus the subject marker 가 (ga), with 저 shifting to 제: 제가 이겼어요 (jega igyeosseoyo) = I won.
만 (man) = only: 게임만 해요 (geimman haeyo) = only plays games.
동안 (dongan) = for, during: 두 시간 동안 (du sigan dongan) = for two hours.
잘 못 (jal mot) = can't do well: 잘 못 불러요 (jal mot bulleoyo) = can't sing well.
스트레스를 풀다 (seuteureseureul pulda) = relieve stress, literally 'untie' it: 스트레스를 풀어요 (seuteureseureul pureoyo).
A -기 (-gi) phrase is a full noun and takes markers like one: 사진 찍기가 (sajin jjikgiga) puts the subject marker 가 (ga) right on 'photo-taking'.
Flat things get the counter 장 (jang) – photos, tickets, paper: 사진을 백 장 (sajineul baek jang) = a hundred photos, literally 'photos, hundred flat-things'.
보다 (boda) alone means 'than' – 더 (deo = more) just adds stress: 카메라보다 더 자주 (kameraboda deo jaju) = more often than the camera.
-(으)러 (-(eu)reo) marks the purpose of going: 배우러 다녀요 (baeureo danyeoyo) = attend in order to learn. It only pairs with movement verbs like 가다 (gada) and 다니다 (danida).
주말 잘 보냈어요? (jumal jal bonaesseoyo?) is literally 'did you spend the weekend well?', a common Monday greeting.
아무것도 + 안 = nothing: 아무것도 안 했어요 (amugeotdo an haesseoyo).
'If' is an ending, not a word: -(으)면 (-(eu)myeon) glues onto the verb – 날씨가 좋으면 (nalssiga joeumyeon) = if the weather is good. No separate 'if' anywhere.
카톡 (katok) = KakaoTalk, Korea's main messaging app – add 하다 (hada) and it turns into a verb: 카톡해요 (katokaeyo) = message me on Kakao.
